<reason>Both sides ran a coherent, well-grounded case built on shared real-world material (Iran, Nigeria, Ecuador, Indonesia). PRO's "design vs implementation" frame gave the cleanest decision rule, and PRO repeatedly rescued its flagship example under direct pressure: Iran's erosion was explained by sanctions rather than instrument failure (and reinforced by the 2019 repeat), while the "where do the savings come from" pressure was answered with the original exclusion-from-top reframe (removing registered vehicles and formal payrolls), which turned CON's "narrow later abandons the motion" attack into a concrete targeting mechanism. CON landed real counterpunches — the permanent-renewal critique of cash, the organized-coalitions answer on durability, and the memorable "fails expensively vs fails silently" weighing — and answered both pressure questions directly. But CON's strongest route, the Iran erosion and fiscal-sequencing arguments, was substantially neutralized, and CON suffered a meaningful execution cost: all four of its long speeches were clipped, including its closing, while only PRO's closing lost text. PRO's closing also crystallized the decisive clash better, reframing CON's "the minister borrows" answer as the whole concession. A close, high-level debate with a clear but competitive edge to PRO.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The oil-doubling-month exchange: B3.1 forced CON to say the finance minister "borrows," and PRO's closing [B5.1] weaponized it — "stability" is an unvoted loan so the SUV's discount doubles while the minibus rider's protection doubles on nothing. Equally decisive was B4.3-B4.4's exclusion-from-top answer, which salvaged the fiscal-savings argument CON had pressed since the pressure questions.</best_rebuttal>
